speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there has been a peaceful demonstration to focus the attention of the public, and especially that of the federal government, on the closing of the Long Point military base. The demonstration in front of the base has just ended.
A few weeks ago, the Minister of National Defence said he was still considering this possibility. This is no time to consider, Mr. Speaker. It is time to act and say no to closing this base, a step that would jeopardize more than 1,000 jobs in East Montreal and more than two million dollars worth of economic spinoffs in the region. East Montreal, as you know is already in poor economic shape, so that closing the base would have a devastating effect.
I therefore wish to ask the government and the Minister of National Defence to inform employees and the people in East Montreal immediately that the base will not be closed and to do so in writing. Only then will businesses, residents and the employees concerned be able to look to the future with confidence.

Mr. Speaker, today, the School of Social Services at the University of Montreal intends to honour Senator Therese Lavoie-Roux for the exceptional contribution she made in the course of her public career, by awarding her an honorary doctorate this afternoon.
Therese Lavoie-Roux was, in the course of her career, first commissioner and then president of the Catholic School Commission of Montreal, MPP for the riding of Acadie, Minister of Health and Social Services, and was recently appointed to the Senate.
Mrs. Lavoie-Roux was the first woman to become Minister of Health and Social Services in Quebec. Mr. Speaker, not enough women accept the challenge of public life, and that is why I think it is very important to emphasize the contribution made by Mrs. Lavoie-Roux and her importance as an example for women who are attracted to public life.
Mr. Speaker, I wish to offer Mrs. Lavoie-Roux my sincere congratulations on receiving her honorary degree this afternoon.

speakeroldname: Mr. Brian L. Gardiner (Prince George-Bulkley Valley):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Forestry is now saying that he only has $100 million to fund a new forest agreement with British Columbia, despite the fact that the entire forestry community is demanding a joint agreement which would include a commitment of $350 million from the federal government.
Mr. Speaker, by buying gas at PetroCan and picking up some forestry stamps, the Boy Scouts are doing more to plant trees in Canada than this government; I will send some stamps to the minister.
Both the federal government and the Socreds in Victoria have failed to sign an agreement despite repeated commitments and promises to do so.
A well-managed forest industry is vital to Canada's economic and environmental well-being, but the health of our forests is left twisting in the wind by the Socreds and Conservatives. They should get on with it and sign a new forest agreement now.

October 24, 1990

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, despite the fact that Canada Post, as a Crown corporation, essentially operates independent of Parliament, on behalf of many residents of Brandon-Souris, I would like to urge Canada Post, in the words of a recent Deloraine Times & Star editorial to "Consult With Your Community".
Although most Canadians are relieved to know that Canada Post no longer requires a $300 or $400-million annual subsidy upon which it used to depend, many rural residents are frustrated and angry with this Crown corporation's recent tendency to reduce both the hours of service and the number of employees without consulting with either the local postmaster or town and rural municipal officials.
If Canada Post officials have sound and logical reasons for the policy changes which they are announcing, they presumably could convince others of the merits of those proposals. To proceed, however, as they are currently doing, without consulting with local leaders, is only to ask for the angry editorial response which many rural weekly newspapers are now providing.

Mr. Speaker, today is United Nations Day, the 45th anniversary of the founding of the United Nations.
In the past half century, the United Nations has had enormous successes and, of course, significant disappointments. The successes include programs of health, aid to refugees, and progress on development. The UN has led the struggle against apartheid and colonialism, has pointed the spotlight on human rights abuses and set the agenda for meeting the terrible and great problems that face the global environment. The end of the cold war holds great hope now that the fundamental purpose of the UN, to establish an international rule of law, can finally be realized.
On United Nations Day, we join with the Secretary General of the UN, Perez de Cuellar, who said, "We must continue to draw inspiration from the ideals to which our Charter gave luminous expression. These ideas are not the intellectual fabrications of visionaries.
We are embedded in the hearts of men and women around the globe".

Mr. Speaker, since this is Small Businesses Week, I would like to draw the attention of the House to the fact that in the past ten years, small businesses have generated exciting ideas and a host of innovative products and services, thus creating thousands of jobs and playing a major role in boosting the economy of this country.
More than ever before, Canadians have realized that entrepreneurship could be exciting and profitable and offer tremendous opportunities for personal enrichment and financial success.
The Small Businesses Loans Act is a federal initiative aimed at helping small businesses, either new or existing ones, to obtain medium-term loans from chartered banks and other designated lending organizations to finance capital improvements.
Under this legislation, the government is committed to reimbursing 85 per cent of the loan to the approved lender, should the borrower default on his payments. This guarantee applies to loans of up to $100,000 for the fiscal year ending on March 31, 1989. More than 17,726 have been granted, representing a total of $682 million.

Mr. Speaker, recently, the Minister of Communications established an advisory committee on la francophonie.
Without wishing to reflect on the competence of the committee's 15 members, I fail to understand why the minister decided that only one Francophone from outside Quebec met his selection criteria and that no members of ethnic minorities qualified for this team of advisers.
Should this not be seen as an insult to Francophones outside Quebec and to new Canadians, including Haitians, Vietnamese, Lebanese, Africans, and so forth, all of whom make a substantial contribution to French culture? How could the government ignore this potential
October 24, 1990

and fail to take advantage of the pluralism that has become one the major elements of our Canadian social fabric, especially in the province of Quebec?
I hope the minister will take steps immediately to correct this oversight, and thus make his committee a more authentic reflection of today's Canada and present to the world an accurate image of what we are. We are very anxious to hear the government's response.

Mr. Speaker, on the occasion of Small Business Week 1990,1 would like to pay tribute to the small business community in Canada, and in particular, to small business in my riding of Delta, British Columbia.
The small business sector has created thousands of jobs and made a major contribution to the Canadian economy. Small and medium-sized businesses have spawned exciting ideas and a host of innovative products and services.
In Delta, we have many examples of new products and technology. Elorizon Fibreglass has created a canopy for the safe transportation of seedlings used for reforestation. MST Products makes specially designed bicycle handle bars to allow cyclists to assume the most aerodynamic position for racing. Sentinel Vision Inc. has developed a unique technology to inspect seams in food and beverage cans for a more efficient quality assurance process.
The federal government, through the Federal Business Development Bank, Western Economic Diversification, and other initiatives, has worked to foster an economic climate in which small business can grow.
Canadian entrepreneurs have seized the opportunities and created their own successes. Small Business Week 1990 celebrates the entrepreneurial spirit and drive behind the success of the small business sector in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, today is United Nations Day and the beginning of UN Disarmament Week.
Faced with the threat of war in the Gulf region, it is imperative that the United Nations be given the support necessary to settle this horrible conflict.
This means we must work within the mandate of the United Nations to make it the co-ordinating body of any military or political action. Otherwise the world will miss this chance to consolidate a new approach to international conflict resolution and peacekeeping.
We must now, more than ever, reject the doctrine of "might is right" and adhere to the rule of law between nations. This could lead, not only to a peaceful resolution in the Gulf, but would help establish an important precedent to prevent and resolve future conflicts.
Let us use this terrible incident as an opportunity to reform and strengthen the United Nations.

Mr. Speaker, as an Anglophone member from Southern Ontario, I would like to congratulate the Premier of the province of Quebec, the hon. Robert Bourassa.
Last Friday, Mr. Bourassa categorically rejected independence for Quebec. He said that Quebecers do not want a Quebec passport and do not want to lose their citizenship. They don't want to lose Canada. Mr. Bourassa also said, with unaccustomed vigour, that he would not compromise Quebec's economic stability.
Personally, Mr. Speaker, I think we need Mr. Bourassa in this great debate on Canada, and as a Canadian, I say: bravo, Mr. Premier!

Mr. Speaker, the Government of Sri Lanka is in the process of committing genocide against the Thmil minority. In my riding there are many constituents of Tamil origin. I have

October 24, 1990
been contacted by many, including the chairman of the National Association of Canadian Tamils, to bring this issue to the attention of the Canadian Parliament.
We in Canada know the problems that can arise with vocal minorities, but we also know that killing the minority group is not the answer.
I ask the House, when will the Secretary of State for External Affairs take appropriate steps to pressure Sri Lanka, which is a member of the British Commonwealth and the United Nations, to stop this outrageous behaviour?
In light of the massive oppression and death that faces Tamil people living in Sri Lanka, I also ask the House to ensure that those who are in need can take refuge in Canada from the brutal regime of the Sri Lankan government.

Mr. Speaker, it's time once again for the corporate welfare bum of the week award.
This week the nominees are BP Canada with $6.2 million in profits in 1989 and no taxes paid; Confederation Life Insurance with $103 million in profits in 1989 and no taxes paid; and last, but by no means least, Domtar with $18 million in profits in 1989, and no taxes paid.
Now for the winner. The envelope, please.
The winner is Domtar. This company along with two other nominees have been outstanding members of Tom d'Aquino's BCNI, but we feel that Domtar deserves special consideration because not only did it have $18 million in profits but on top of that it received an extra $21 million in tax credits from this government. With that kind of business savvy, Domtar deserves a b rating.

Mr. Speaker, at a time when thousands of workers are losing their jobs in
Atlantic Canada, it is unbelievable that this government, through Bill C-21, will inflict more hardship on Canadians struggling with high interest rates, the proposed goods and services tax and a made-in-Canada recession.
The government adds insult to injury by eliminating its financial contribution to the UI fund, while at the same time maintaining control over the allocation of money collected from workers and employers.
In its arrogance, the government will take our money, do with it as it pleases, and leave the regions, such as Atlantic Canada, with added strain on their already fragile provincial economies.
With the passage of Bill C-21 and if the unemployment rate remains stable, Prince Edward Islanders will receive only 35 weeks of benefits rather than the 42 weeks received under the old system.
At the same time, they will have to work two extra weeks to qualify for fewer benefits. This means that Islanders must now find an additional nine weeks of work.

At long last, Mr. Speaker, Bill C-21 has been given royal assent after a long stay in the other place. Our government is satisfied with this turn of events because we are now in a better position to help Canadian workers acquire new skills and plan for the future.
Several amendments will make it easier for workers to cope successfully with ever changing labour market conditions. These amendments also bring unemployment insurance provisions in line with the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms.
Mr. Speaker, the amendments reflect the government's labour force enhancement strategy and make the unemployment insurance program more atuned to the priorities of workers seeking assistance and vocational training.
October 24, 1990

speakeroldname: Hon. Herb Gray (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Finance.
Today, the government's own figures show that bankruptcies are up 37 per cent. In the face of this, the minister has the nerve to send out 40,000 videos to try to tell Canadians that they are among "the most fortunate people on earth".
Why does the Minister of Finance think that the thousands of Canadians going into bankruptcy, losing their jobs, their businesses, and their farms are among the most fortunate people on earth? Why does he not stop this phoney propaganda campaign and bring in new policies that will turn this economy around, and not drive it into the ground?
Hear, hear.

Mr. Speaker, I say to you again that Canadians are one of the most favoured people in the world today.
We are going through a difficult period in the economy. There is no question of that. I have been talking about that for a number of months now. I am not happy about it. But when you stand back, Mr. Speaker, and look at the advantages that we have in this country and when you look at the challenges that we are facing in relation to the major difficulties and disruptions that are going on in other countries of the world, you have to reflect on the fact that we are a very fortunate people.
It is very important as that very fortunate people to do the things that are right and to follow the sound economic policies that we have been following to get our economy back on track so we can continue to do more to help those in other countries.
In the meantime, we have our work cut out here. We are sticking to our guns on it, because we believe that it is the right thing to get our economy on track again.

Hear, hear.
Oral Questions

speakeroldname: Hon. Herb Gray (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, what will it take for this minister to recognize and admit the damage his policies are doing to our farmers, our business people, and our workers? Do they have to start sending him videos showing themselves losing their farms, their businesses, their homes, and their jobs. If they did, those videos would be rated r for recession to show the horror of the government's policies.
When will the minister stop trying to defend, as he is doing now, the policies that got us into this mess and start trying to do something constructive about it?

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member has referred to this video. The video is designed to respond to questions that people have been asking us. We have had 350,000 odd people who have called the information line. They want to know about the GST. They want to know where the GST fits into our economic plan. They want to know what we are doing to control government spending. They want to get an accurate picture of the financial position of the federal government, and that is precisely what this video is designed to do.
I would also say to my hon. friend that he has a short-term point of view here. I do not deny it is a view which shows that we have a difficult period in the economy. If he would extend his view to the last five or six years when the same policies that we have been following have resulted in record rates of growth, growth that is second only to Japan of the major industrialized countries and growth that has resulted in the creation of over 1.5 million jobs.
That is the combination of policies that the government has been following that has got us to a position where we have had a very good economy over the past six years. We have to get through this period. If we can get through this period, get the rate of inflation down, and get the inflationary pressures under control, then we can build the base for strong non-inflationary growth into the future.

speakeroldname: Hon. Herb Gray (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Canadians are losing their farms, their businesses and their jobs because of the policies of this

October 24, 1990
Oral Questions
minister. Meanwhile the Minister of Finance is wasting public funds on a video which shows nothing of the economic mess his policies helped create.
Again I ask the Minister of Finance when will he recall that video and come up with a policy designed to pull Canadians out of the recession?

Mr. Speaker, I am not going to withdraw the video because the video is responding to the concerns and questions of many people in the country. I will send the hon. member a video later this afternoon, if he wishes. I will send one to my colleague, the Leader of the New Democratic Party. It is important for all members of Parliament to learn what is happening.
The title of the video is Where Do Your Tax Dollars Go? I think there are a lot of Canadians who are asking that question. They have seen increases in taxation, which my hon. friend has commented on on a number of occasions. It is important to know what those tax dollars are spent on, the impact of the debt that we inherited in 1984 on the spending of the government, and the impact of the compound interest which we inherited in 1984. That compound interest, by the way, represents 80 per cent of the accumulation of debt that we have seen since 1984.
The hon. Leader of the Opposition should understand that it was the government that he was associated with which laid the groundwork for the high interest rates that we are facing.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Indian and Northern Affairs. On September 25, the Prime Minister spoke of his commitment to accelerating the specific land claims process. The aboriginal peoples of the Atlantic provinces have yet to be convinced of this commitment.
The maritime chiefs are meeting in Moncton, New Brunswick this week, including the chief from the Woodstock Band whose specific claim was validated by the government six years ago with no progress to date.
How does the minister intend to accelerate the specific claims process in the Atlantic regions of Canada?

speakeroldname: Hon. Thomas Siddon (Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development):
speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, consistent with the Prime Minister's commitment, we have been holding meetings with various groups with a view to expediting the settlement of treaty deficiencies and the comprehensive claims. Such was the discussion in which the Prime Minister participated yesterday in Vancouver. It was a very successful meeting with the combined leadership of all of the native leadership of British Columbia.
Two weeks ago in this city, with members of Atlantic chiefs present, a process was undertaken with a view to improving the processing of specific claims. The government will certainly be bringing forward a major initiative in that respect, hopefully before the end of this year.

Mr. Speaker, my supplementary question is directed to the same minister.
In excess of 500 specific claims remain unsettled to this day in Canada. In New Brunswick alone over 68 claims remain outstanding. A year and a half ago the government refused a proposal for funding for land claims from the Union of New Brunswick Indians and has not responded to a re-application for funding submitted one year ago.
Is this what the Prime Minister means by acceleration, a system that cannot provide a response to a serious request and a Conservative member of Parliament who refuses to meet with the chief of that reserve?

speakeroldname: Hon. Thomas Siddon (Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development):
speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would urge the hon. member to show as much confidence in our ability to deal with these issues as the native leadership of Canada has done. They are participating in important meetings and have promised me a report within 30 days on the process which will be required to improve our ability to dispose of specific claims quickly.
I myself have met with the chief of the Woodstock band to get on with the process that the Liberal government was unable to complete over many years when the party of which she is a member was in office.
October 24, 1990

Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Minister of Finance about the record number of bankruptcies.
In the previous worst year, 1982, when the minister was in opposition, he said: "This government must begin to realize that it is individual people who are being hurt." He went on to say: "We must deal with individual Canadians who are losing their jobs and their businesses."
Will the minister back up his caring words from then with action now to respond to this record 37 per cent increase in bankruptcies in the country?
Hear, hear.

Mr. Speaker, I understand that it is people who are losing those businesses. I understand that the people who are working at those firms are losing their jobs, and I do not take any pleasure in that. I do not enjoy that at all.
What I have to point out to the hon. member, as he makes reference to 1981-1982, is that the level of bankruptcies as a percentage of the economy is about half what it was at that time.
The other point that I would make to him is that, if we are going to be able to get through this period and avoid the excessives of the high interest rates of 22 per cent and 25 per cent that we endured in 1981-1982, it is important for us to get the inflationary pressures under of control. That is why we have been following the policies that we have been following. We are making some progress there. We are getting those inflationary pressures under control. As we do so, we will be able to see some reduction in interest rates.
If we let the party go on, as was the case in 1981-1982, then the hon. member is asking for exactly the sort of thing we want to avoid here. Mr. Speaker, we are determined to avoid that.

Mr. Speaker, it is very clear that the minister has lost those caring attitudes that he expressed in 1982.
Paul Cazabon is a farmer in St. Joachim in my constituency who has lost his 740 acre farm because of high interest rates on his machinery, his land, and his operating loans. That is what these bankruptcy statistics mean. They mean broken dreams for people right across the country.
Oral Questions
I want to ask the Prime Minister directly: What has the Prime Minister of the country to say to Paul Cazabon and his family?

Mr. Speaker, Paul Cazabon is someone for whom I have a great deal of sympathy and the difficulties that he is going through. But if we do not do the things we are doing, there will be many more Paul Cazabons who will be suffering from the same sort of interest rates that we had in 1981-1982. Surely, my hon. friend must recognize that that is something that we want to avoid. We must avoid. That is why we are following the directions we are now.
As I have indicated on many occasions, we are making progress. If we continue to make progress, we are going to see many fewer people such as Paul Cazabon suffering from the things he is going through now. Those difficulties are very, very difficult for him. I understand that, but we want to stop this happening in the future. The best thing we can do to stop that happening in the future is get the problems under control, as we seem to be getting those problems under control.

I cannot believe that this minister is telling us the best that he can do is to see an increase of 7,000 in bankruptcy statistics this year. Why can this minister and this Prime Minister not give us some sensitive, caring answers? Instead of action to help Paul Cazabon, the minister is spending another $300,000 on a video.
I ask this minister-

What explanation does the minister have for wasting this kind of money when so many Canadians have gone bankrupt this year?

As I
indicated in my previous answer, Mr. Speaker, I do not take any pleasure in seeing what Paul Cazabon is going through now, but I do know that in the province of Ontario there are a lot fewer Paul Cazabons than there were as recently as 1986. The 1986 statistics show 71 farm

October 24, 1990
Oral Questions
bankruptcies. That reached a low point of 12 in Ontario in 1989. It is up to 19 this year.
The point that I am making is that we are trying hard to make progress. We have put out additional funds, additional support for the farm community through interest-free advances. We are fighting the battles at the GATT to make sure that we have the international problems as well looked after as we can as one single country. We are introducing the goods and services tax that for the farm community will result in a savings in aggregate across the country of $250 million. That is a major assist for the farm community and it will help keep the Paul Cazabons of this countiy from going over the edge into bankruptcy.
That is an indication of the commitment that we have as a government to dealing with the problems in the farm community today.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the minister of energy. The minister is fresh from a meeting with representatives from Canadian oil companies and consumer groups. Given the continued high price of gasoline and the fact that oil companies want to raise prices even higher, with the minister's blessing, adding to their soaring profits, did the minister express to the oil companies his desire to see an immediate decrease in the price of gasoline to bring it in line with the lower oil prices on the world market?

speakeroldname: Hon. Jake Epp (Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yes, I did meet with the oil companies, as well as consumer groups. I point out to the hon. member what has been said here many times. That is in the Canadian system of accounting for the price of oil at the gas pumps, there is a 60 to 90 day lag. I have said also to the oil companies that I do not expect them to take any advantage of the situation. We discussed that with the consumer groups as well.
In fact, if the hon. member takes a look at the profit pictures, for example, today, I think it is fair to say that one has to look at more than one quarter, if he looks at the downstream side. The figures are different, for example, on the upstream side, depending on the price
of crude that went into the system and the price of crude that went into the refining process.

Mr. Speaker, I have a supplementary for the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs. Yesterday, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources gave this House the assurance, and with him his colleague, the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs, that he was watching energy costs very closely. The minister is of course aware that his department has already received a number of complaints from Canadian consumers. I would like to ask the Minister whether there is any evidence of fraud. If so, could the minister inform this House of the facts in this respect?

speakeroldname: Hon. Pierre Blais (Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs and Minister of State (Agriculture)):
speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs; Minister of State (Agriculture)
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the Bureau of Competition Policy is responsible for examining each case brought to its attention. It has a monitoring role and receives information similar to that just given by the hon. member. In fact, all members of this House have a joint responsibility, if they have the slightest impression or if they have any evidence that might lead one to believe that something is wrong or that there is a failure to comply with the Competition Act, to get in touch with the Director of the Bureau of Competition Policy and give him those facts, to avoid any public perception that there could be abuse in this area. If you have any facts, it is up to you to meet the Director of the Bureau of Competition Policy and give him the facts, and he will investigate the matter. That is his responsibility, Mr. Speaker, and I can assure you that he will do what is necessary.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the minister responsible for seniors. The minister is surely aware of the number of Canadian senior citizens who live at or below the poverty line. Indeed almost 40 per cent of single seniors live below the poverty line. How can the minister justify the imposition of the goods and services tax on simple things like
October 24, 1990

band-aids and aspirin, which many seniors take to prevent heart attacks?

speakeroldname: Hon. Monique Vezina (Minister of State (Employment and Immigration) and Minister of State (Seniors)):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Seniors); Minister of State (Employment and Immigration)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, to me social justice means helping people who really need it and this is what our government is doing with the GST. We want to share the tax revenue and seniors will be protected within this process.
Our government and myself, as Minister responsible for the rights and also for the responsibilities of older people, are working to help those in need including senior citizens.

Mr. Speaker, my supplementary is to the same minister. We all know that visiting the doctor is quite expensive for our health care system. Can the minister explain the fact that according to the GST Information Office, a cane or safety bars bought with a prescription is tax-free, but if a person walks in off the street to buy the same item, the GST is charged.

speakeroldname: Hon. Monique Vezina (Minister of State (Employment and Immigration) and Minister of State (Seniors)):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Seniors); Minister of State (Employment and Immigration)
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I remind the hon. Member that essential goods will not be taxed and that purchasing power will be the same and even higher for seniors. We are listening to them and trying to help them fill their needs.

Mr. Speaker, in Vancouver yesterday the Prime Minister committed his government to resolving native land claims and to priorizing native issues.
On November 10, the Innu of Labrador will be marching on Ottawa to advance their land claims and to protest Canada's decision to triple low level military flights over their homelands.
My question to the Prime Minister is this. Is his government prepared to extend the same commitment
Oral Questions
to the Innu of Labrador that he extended to natives in B.C.; that is, to settle their land claim fairly and expeditiously and to deal fairly with their objections against low level military test flights.

speakeroldname: Hon. Bill McKnight (Minister of National Defence):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member is using statements and numbers that are not accurate, and he knows they are not accurate.
What he does know, Mr. Speaker, is that there has been a decision taken by NATO not to proceed with the NATO tactical fighter centre. He knows that. The Innu know that. We understand, as he does, that there is an overlapping claim. There already are Indian claims, the CAM group and the Labrador Inuit Association which are being addressed by my colleague.
If the Innu of Labrador would use the dollars that the Government of Canada provided to research their claim and submit that claim to the Government of Canada, I am sure the government would look at it and take action.

Mr. Speaker, I have a supplementary to the Prime Minister.
The Lubicon people of northwestern Alberta have been waiting for over half a century for a just settlement of their legitimate land claims. All they have received is neglect at best, and wholly unreasonable take-it-or-leave it offers at worst.
Again arising out of the Prime Minister's remarks in B.C. yesterday, when will the government give substance to the Prime Minister's words by starting to bargain in good faith with the Lubicon people? Will the government, when it does so, agree to use the Lubicons' June 1 Draft Settlement Agreement as the basis for that bargaining?

speakeroldname: Hon. Thomas Siddon (Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development):
speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member knows of this government's commitment to deal with comprehensive and specific claims. Of course, we have been engaged in serious negotiation of the Lubicon claim, at least up until the time last June where that negotiation was suspended. I might remind the hon. member that a United Nations committee, looking into a grievance of the Lubicon, indicated that the federal government was taking an appropriate approach to negotiating and resolving this claim. Finally, I remind the hon. member that the Lubicon demand is vastly in excess

October 24, 1990

of the settlement which has been achieved with most other native communities in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, my question is to the minister responsible for small businesses. The Canadian Federation of Independent Business released a study yesterday showing that small businesses along our borders from coast to coast are being adversely affected by our tax system. The threat of the GST is going to further complicate this. What does the minister responsible for small businesses say about those tens of thousands of small businesses that are being destroyed by this government's tax policy?

speakeroldname: Hon. Tom Hockin (Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would remind all of those border communities that the federal government is putting in place, under the GST, a rebate system for everything that visitors from the United States and other countries buy and take home. They get a complete rebate. We are making it very easy for them to apply for it through the duty-free shops. That is the best possible answer for our retailers.

Mr. Speaker, I am not sure that the minister heard my question. The point is that a baby suit or a baby jacket is the same in Buffalo as it is in Toronto, Vancouver or Montreal. There is only one thing which is different; it is the price. What ideas does he have to put forward to keep those purchases in Canada?

speakeroldname: Hon. Tom Hockin (Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank my hon. friend and congratulate him on his appointment as critic for small business and entrepreneurship. I am glad that he is trying to be creative, especially on this important issue. What is happening here, though, is that the manufacturers' sales tax is being removed for the first time in 65 years. The manufacturers' sales tax will lower the cost of running every single business in Canada, plus foreign tourists will be getting the rebate.
More important, the CFIB made the point yesterday that it feels the level of taxation is too heavy across Canada; municipal, provincial and federal. It believes that the municipal role is even higher than the federal role. We believe in working with the border communi
ties, as we have through our border community task force, to find ways to better market our products, to better position our products, and to help the small business community of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, more than a year ago it was a tough-talking government that proclaimed its intention to clear the refugee backlog with a new refugee system. Instead, what it has created is a monster that tortures claimants and their families with long delays, will eat hundreds of millions of taxpayers dollars and probably give birth to a backlog of its very own.
What is the Prime Minister doing about what has been so aptly described as his Minister of Immigration's costly flop of a program?

speakeroldname: Hon. Monique Vezina (Minister of State (Employment and Immigration) and Minister of State (Seniors)):

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
On September 28, 1990, the hon. member for Shefford rose on a question of privilege concerning a statement made by the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources announcing the launch of the Hibernia Development Project, the press release of that statement and certain news reports based on the announcement. The hon. member compared this situation to the

October 24, 1990
Privilege
question of privilege concerning the advertising of the Goods and Services Thx and my ruling of October 10, 1989.
I would like to take this opportunity at the outset to thank all those hon. members who made interventions: the hon. member for Shefford; the Parliamentary Secretary to the Government House Leader; the hon. member for Kamloops; and the hon. member for Humber-St. Barbe-Baie Verte.

In his presentation the hon. member for Shefford described quite succinctly the situation which existed last year regarding the goods and service tax advertising campaign and accurately summarized the Chair's ruling on that very serious matter. He then went on to liken the situation in 1989 to the September 14 statement of the hon. Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources and its coverage by some of the media.
I would like to thank the hon. member for providing the Chair with a copy of the minister's statement which I have read very carefully.
The hon. member pointed out that certain television reports indicated that the project would begin immediately. He also stated that the premier of Newfoundland had said that Bill C-44, the Hibernia Act, had already been passed. The crux of the hon. member's argument was that the press release and the way it was reported gave the public the impression that the government was using Parliament as a rubber stamp. Parliament was being disregarded and ignored unless all parliamentarians were being insulted.

As was the case with the GST advertisements, the Chair must look at two issues. First of all, has there been a breach of privilege insofar as the press release and certain media reports prejudice the work of the House? Secondly, does this matter constitute a contempt of Parliament because it is inferred that the House is merely a rubber stamp with no role to play in the final go ahead of the Hibernia Project? I would refer hon. members to my lengthy ruling of October 10, 1989, on the GST advertisements and to the ruling of December 18, 1989, on a related question.
While superficially there may be a similarity between these issues, at their heart the two situations are very different.

Having read the Hibernia development press release and some of the media reports, as well as the testimony of the hon. Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources before the legislative committee on Bill C-44 and before the Standing Committee on Energy, Mines and Resources, it is abundantly clear to the Chair that there was no attempt on anyone's part to mislead this House, or to imply that the passage of Bill C-44 was a fait accompli. The thrust of the press release of the minister's statement was that the Government of Canada and the other parties to the project had resolved all outstanding issues in their negotiations and that agreements binding all parties had been completed. These agreements would, to quote the press release, and I am now quoting exactly the press release, "now go into escrow, where they will be held by an independent third party until they can be signed formally following the passage of Bill C-44, the Hibernia Act, by Parliament this fall".

The statement leaves no impression that legislation has not been submitted to Parliament. The reference to the role of Parliament is not ambiguous and even press reports noted that the completion of the deal was contingent on the passage by Parliament of the enabling legislation.

One aspect of this issue which may appear confusing to the media and the general public is the fact that work is beginning on this project before Bill C-44 has been enacted. As the Parliamentary Secretary to the Government House Leader and the hon. member for Humber- St. Barbe-Baie Verte both pointed out, start-up funding for the project from the Canada-Newfoundland Offshore Development Fund has already been approved by Parliament. This was also pointed out in the minister's statement. The hon. member for Humber-St. Barbe- Baie Verte also noted, quite rightly, that if Bill C-44 is not enacted, the project will be shut down when it runs out of interim financing.
October 24, 1990



It is contingent on all levels of government, on parliamentarians and on the media to explain to Canadians, as carefully and completely as possible, complex issues such as the funding of the Hibernia Development Project. It is my view that the minister's press release was careful (in tone and content) and clearly respected the role of the House of Commons. Accordingly I must rule that there is no prima facie case of privilege.

As a former chairman of the Committee on Fisheries, Forestry and the Environment, I feel that perhaps what is already in existence is probably good enough to start with and that we should make it stronger rather than weaker. This bill is not strong enough. I just want to explain the reasons why I feel that what is already in existence is strong enough. The departments and the responsible authorities, perhaps, did not realize there are already, in existence, guidelines that have to be followed.
I had a very real experience in my own constituency which started in the summer of 1988 with an ACOA grant, of all things. No one would think that the giving of an ACOA grant would be of such importance to residents of a given community and create such a stir. This happened to be an ACOA grant for an aggregates plant in Southwest Nova. This plant grinds rock and makes gravel and entails a lot of run-off and a lot of air pollution because of the crusher and other equipment. The grant was substantial. We do not get too many grants of that size. The grant from ACOA was over $800,000.
At the time, I suggested that there should have been an environmental impact study on the giving of money under that grant to that particular site in view of the public concern, which was given no opportunity to be aired.
Oddly enough, the grant was announced in September. The Department of the Environment satisfied itself with ACOA action in a letter in November of that year after the grant had been approved, but before funds had been given out. I thought every opportunity should have been taken by the Department of the Environment or at least have a hearing to allow the people to state their concerns over the giving of public money for a project where there was definitely opposition.
The odd thing that happened after the little encounter that I had with the Department of the Environment and ACOA was that on May 22, 1990, an exclusion list was put forward under the existing law. We have an environmental assessment and review process, and yet we have an exclusion list brought forward by ACOA for any future funding. It presented its exclusion list to the Department of the Environment.
This is exactly what is wrong with this bill. There is not enough power in the Ministry of the Environment, or the new agency', to totally reject a project and force the Governor in Council, cabinet, to defend a decision that is contradictory to a review recommendation or where the Minister of the Environment or the agency which will be set up under this bill could totally reject the project. Then we would have to see the basis of whatever the cabinet felt was the values involved in the project in order to go ahead with funding.
That, in my opinion, is what is lacking. There are no teeth in this bill to make the government accountable for a project in which it is overstepping the bounds of its own act.
Let me tell you that the definition within the bill is very commendable. The preamble is very commendable. The purposes of the bill are commendable. You can summarize clause 4 in three parts: first, to ensure the careful consideration of the environmental effect of federal projects; second, to encourage actions which promote and maintain both a healthy economy and a healthy environment; and third, to safeguard against serious transporter environmental effects.
We have gone over the Rafferty-Alameda dam project in this House and we have seen the ineptitude throughout the whole process with the courts saying that a review should have been done before the federal government took part in that process, issued the licences or gave out any money of any type. There was no review in the court sent to the government.
Today, we have a government that is scared to take away the licence of that project because on one hand, it is scared to do it, and on the other hand, it has not followed its own process. It may have a contract, and it may have set up a review process. Obviously, something is wrong when there is this mix-up what with continuation of that dam project that we have seen in the last two
October 24, 1990

weeks, and the Saskatchewan government totally ignoring the federal Minister of the Environment.
I cannot emphasize enough that this bill does not allow the agency to reject outright a project. It only allows the agency to review a project after the project manager, the responsible authority, the government department that wants to fund that project, after that government department does the screening. That is the way I understand it. The agency can say it goes along with whatever the recommendations are, and there is no need to go further. If it says some areas are being violated, it can set a mediation or a panel review. But at no point in the screening can it reject it totally. There must a mediation or a review panel.
The whole object of this bill is to try to find a negotiated settlement to environmental concerns. I do not think that the people in Canada want to see negotiated settlements if there are real concerns about the environment with respect to projects funded by this federal government.
I congratulate them that it put in a section so that we can get into discussions with provinces as to concerns over jurisdiction and transboundary concerns with the Americans on joint projects and studies. That will happen only if those parties want to become a party to the federal process. This bill will be studied again, but there are so many things that weaken it that I truly feel that a prestudy of the bill should have been done before second reading.
Some of the things that weaken it are references to being able to set up mandatory lists of projects, exclusions to lists that must be reviewed and the criteria of what will, under regulations, be excluded. I refer to clause 5 of the bill where there are projects to be assessed. There are four subclauses to clause 5. These are the type of projects that should be assessed: a project proposed by a federal authority; a project financed in whole or in part by a federal authority, unless a project was not identified at the time of financing and the federal authority would have no power with respect to the project after it was identified; a project requiring the transfer or lease of lands by a federal authority unless the project was not identified at the time of the transfer, and a project for which a federal authority issues a permit or a licence, grants an approval or takes any other
Government Orders
action in order to facilitate the project. These are the things which would trigger the projects that should be assessed. Then you go to clause 55 and these are the regulations. It refers to the Governor in Council. That is our cabinet or any cabinet of the day, which has a great discretion. I pick out three of the clauses that it may make regulations about.
Under subclause (b) it may make regulations about prescribing a list of projects or classes of projects for which an environmental assessment is not required where the Governor in Council or the cabinet of the day is of the opinion that the environmental effects of the project are likely to be negligible.
What is negligible? Negligible to someone in downtown Toronto may be a $1 million project. In South West Nova that may affect 120 families. That might be negligible to someone in Ottawa. It is not negligible to the people in rural Canada. It is not negligible if it is going to destroy the value of their homes, their wealth and their environment. That is what that ACOA grant did.
Under the present rules, they were able to put in an exclusion list as of May 22, 1990. I am sure no one at ACOA ever thought that their projects had to be screened. I remember, having been on the committee when that regulation was passed or prior to it being passed, that any government project had to be looked at to see if there was an environmental effect and, if so, what effect it would have in the dispensing of that money.
So, negligible in clause 55 has a lot of interpretation. A $1 million grant might be negligible in Edmonton, but it is not negligible in southwestern Nova Scotia. If you talk to the people in Lockeport today, you will know that $1 million will go a long way toward helping them achieve some type of stability in restoring their livelihood.
Subclause (d) prescribes a list of projects, or classes of projects, for which an environmental assessment is not required. Remember this is the governor in council, not the agency. If you gave the new agency the ability to decide this, you might feel that they were putting the environment first, rather than a cabinet formed from different responsible authorities and different departments, as under the act. This is giving it to the governor

October 24, 1990
Government Orders
in council, it is not giving it to the new agency. The governor in council in subclause (d) may make regulations prescribing a list of projects, or classes of projects, for which an environmental assessment is not required, where the governor in council-and remember, Mr. Speaker, we only have one minister from Nova Scotia- is of the opinion that the contribution of the responsible authority to the projects through the exercise of its powers or the performance of its duties or functions is minimal.
I wonder what it would do with Point Aconi where it was only the Department of Fisheries that had a federal responsibility in the environmental process. I wonder what it would do with the Nova Scotia tidal power project that is in existence today and kills thousands of fish. The government was told in the past that that project would kill fish. It also caused erosion. The government is going to make it into a sanctuary for ducks now that the fish are destroyed in the river. There would not have to be a review because it might be considered minimal in the sense that this government's policy as it relates to fish is anything goes.
Look at the west coast. We saw it last week. Look at Point Aconi. There was no problem with the fisheries and obviously it is a prescribed attitude of this government that if it does not affect the big, then it will not worry about the small. If the big companies are not complaining, it will not worry about the small people who may complain. We just have to look at free trade and the ads about that, even though communities are dying because of the free trade agreement.
I want to go back to the responsible authority and describe for my constituents and others across Canada what happens. The responsible authority, the departmental minister or deputy minister, or someone, because not all projects go to the ministerial level, screens the project, sends it to the agency and the agency either sets up mediation or a review panel if the agency feels there should be one. If the agency feels that there is nothing wrong with it, it can go ahead as long as there is public notice given, and public notice in Canada means The Canada Gazette. Ordinary Canadians do not read that gazette to find out what the Government of Canada is proposing. Unless there is someone who wants to talk about it, who wants to bring it to the attention of people, we will not know, because if it goes back to ACOA, it does not have to tell anyone who it will fund or what it
will give. It is usually after the fact, after the announcement that you get the concerns of the people.
The Minister of Finance may like this legislation because he has more control over the costs of expensive review processes. I have seen expensive review processes happen. I have seen one happen in the last few years. A most qualified group of people looked at it and gave a report that was positive. Yet we will never have that type of review again. The government would not follow it because it had its own agenda.
As long as we give no power to the agency to reject totally, let the Governor in Council defend the project for Canadian people and then let the Canadian people decide if a decision of the Governor in Council is right or wrong, if that power were in the bill, I could go along with its purposes.
However, as long as they narrow the purposes of this bill so that there are no teeth in it, there is something wrong with trying to pass it when there is already a process in existence requiring every agency in the federal government, before they take part in any project, to have a review of the project as it affects the environment. If they are not going to give it teeth, I think we should go with the status quo, and we know the courts have said that they must have a review.

Mr. Speaker, I listened with care to the hon. member's speech on this important bill. I am encouraged to hear that she also is opposed to the passage of the bill in its present form.
The deficiencies in Bill C-78 are evident for anyone who has read the bill, although there was a lot of hype when the bill was first introduced and there was a lot of hope among Canadians that we would finally have a real environmental assessment process to meet the challenges that face us in the 1990s and on.
Some of the deficiencies that are evident are in the whole process design of environmental assessment. The process must be effective in guiding and encouraging and, where necessary, forcing environmental responsibility into all stages of the conception, planning, and approval of environmentally significant undertakings.
The member was speaking as a member from Atlantic Canada. She mentioned the Point Aconi process where it is evident that the environmental assessment was not followed. There is another Atlantic Canada initiative, the whole Hibernia undertaking. There is a significant
October 24, 1990

amount of taxpayers' money going into it, and there is no test of sustainability in either one of those projects.
I would like her comments on particularly the Hibernia project involving billions, of taxpayers' dollars. We know who pays the majority of the taxes in this country. It is ordinary Canadians, to a far greater degree than large corporations. I would like her response to those two projects, Hibernia and Point Aconi.

Mr. Speaker, I welcome the member's question. I will say this about Hibernia: we in the east do not get too many major projects. This is one of them. Oil and gas in the east is perhaps one of the future areas of development, particularly if we relate it to the fisheries, what is happening on the east coast, and this government's attitude toward the fisheries.
In oil and gas there have been effective actions on the environment on Georges Bank. When it wanted to put an oil rig there or go out to look for development, the people in the area rejected it. The fishermen rejected it. The citizens in the southern end that I represent did such a fine job of opposing it that there were no rigs on Georges Bank.
There have been studies on Hibernia. I am not as close to Hibernia as I am to Sable Island or to Georges Bank.
If there are people in Newfoundland who are satisfied with the process that was used on Hibernia, and the government is satisfied with the process, then I cannot say-and I have not seen too many people in the east opposed to the process used on Hibernia, and I say that quite honestly-they have weighed the environmental consequences of the development of Hibernia.
I might have a different view from some of the people who are going ahead with it. I also know that at one time the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources was doing some of the exploration for oil and gas on the east coast. There were studies done about what was to be done in the event of a crisis in the water in the future: who was to pay the costs, and things like that. I know that there was a very intensive study done. I know that every
Government Orders
segment of industry on the east coast took part as far as Hibernia was concerned.
I can agree that as a federal government or a provincial government we do not make people aware enough of just what is going to happen and whether or not our decisions are based on a full evaluation of the consequences. I say this because people do look at the jobs that can be created. That is the present day concern. The review process, the safeguards, and the safety nets were not considered in the process before.
As far as some of the fines and the penalties that were brought in for any sort of destruction of the environment by oil companies are concerned, they have been set in the process. Maybe after five or six years we should be looking at some of it in terms of the destructiveness of such a project.
I certainly am well aware that the Canadian public is never as aware as it should be until after the fact. I do not know if there is not a role in here for doing this. I welcome in this act the follow-up to anything that has been reviewed and anything the mediator or the review panel has put in; but people must know that there is a follow-up program and what their rights are under it.
As well, under this bill there is a fund for people to take action. We do not know how much money will be put into the fund, whether it is only an injunction or whether one can proceed right to the Supreme Court. I can only say that there is a lot more we can do to make people aware and allow people to weigh the consequences of a decision by cabinet, by governments, whether provincial or federal, as to their environment.
In my own province they may not follow it, but at least there is a guideline that people know each step of the way where to go to intervene, as is being done presently for development on Digby Neck.

speakeroldname: Mr. Lee Clark (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of the Environment):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in light of the fact that I am sure the hon. member has studied the bill with care, I find it difficult to understand how she could reach the conclusion that this was, in her words, "toothless legislation", particularly in light of the fact that those who are writing on behalf of the Dutch government-and I think that we all understand that the Dutch government has a world-wide reputation for being leaders in the field of environmental protection-wrote a letter of August 3 to Mr. Robinson who is in charge of FEARO. They said in part:
Bill C-78, it is not the most exciting name but the content counts.
We, the whole EIA-department, would like to congratulate you and
FEARO with this milestone.
They continued:

Government Orders
These new elements will bring Canada back to the lead in EIA
regulation! And give us inspiration for new developments.
That is an extremely noteworthy compliment to be received from a government for which we at least on this side of the House have a great deal of respect. With all deference to the hon. member, it would seem to me that this individual who is head of EIA department in the Dutch government is an individual whose views I would certainly hold in great esteem. I am wondering how the contrast could be so great.

Holland, Mr. Speaker, is a very small country. Its government may think that this legislation looks good and maybe it would like to have it there. However, this legislation is not as strong as the existing guidelines wherein one had to do something in order to be in compliance with them.
This time the responsible authority will screen. It will go to the agency. The agency will make a decision as to how much further it goes, but the agency does not have the teeth to reject. I do not see that it has much power.

Mr. Speaker, I want to follow along on that point because we have seen the track record of this government when it comes to national standards. It seems to retreat from national standards.
I want to cite specifically Bill C-29 respecting the forestry act wherein we have a definition of sustainable development. That is the national standard. Presumably Bill C-29 is the national forestry standard for this country which has been put forward by this government. Time after time we have seen where the provincial standard is lower and yet our standard is subservient.
Does the member not think that without the necessary teeth to rule supreme on this act we are going to see a situation evolve across this country where we have 10,11, or 12 different standards?

Mr. Speaker, I thank my colleague for his question. I would say definitely we will have 12 different standards. The most important point about this legislation is that if the government of the day decides that water is not important then chances are it is going to destroy the water.
It allows the Governor in Council to make the ultimate power to control the process. I think we should have the guts, the boldness, and the leadership in a country this size, with the natural resources at our
disposal, to enhance our environmental review process, and to give the minister or this new agency sole discretion to make the decision as to the effect on the environment that the project will have, and then have the government have the guts to say to the people: "We are going against that."
